title: Test Your Understanding: Event Sourcing and CQRS
description: Event logs, aggregates, projections, and read/write split — trade-offs, not buzzwords.

questions.question: In event sourcing, the primary source of truth is:

options.text: The latest row in a normalized CRUD table
The append-only log of events that happened
The read model used by the query API
The snapshot table updated on every write

questions.explanation: Events are immutable facts appended to a store. Current state and read models are derived by applying or projecting those events. Snapshots optimize replay; they do not replace the log as authority.

questions.question: What is the main role of an aggregate in event sourcing?

options.text: To join data from every table in the system in one transaction
To define a consistency boundary and enforce invariants before events append
To replace the need for read models
To batch events from unrelated customers for throughput

questions.explanation: An aggregate (e.g. one Order) owns one event stream. Commands validate against current state inside that boundary. Cross-aggregate rules use sagas or async coordination, not one giant transaction.

questions.question: CQRS primarily separates:

options.text: SQL from NoSQL
Commands (writes) from queries (reads) with potentially different models
Synchronous from asynchronous HTTP
Primary from replica databases only

questions.explanation: CQRS optimizes write and read paths independently. You can use CQRS without event sourcing (e.g. CDC to a read DB). Event sourcing often pairs with CQRS because append-only writes and rich queries want different shapes.

questions.question: Why are snapshots used in event-sourced systems?

options.text: To delete old events for compliance
To avoid replaying every event from the beginning on each load
To make events mutable for corrections
To eliminate the need for projectors

questions.explanation: Rebuilding from event #1 every time does not scale. Snapshots persist aggregate state at version N; only events after N are replayed. If a snapshot is wrong, the event log still allows full rebuild.

questions.question: A read model updated by a projector is typically:

options.text: Strongly consistent with the write side at all times
Eventually consistent — may lag behind appended events
The legal system of record for audits
Updated by mutating events in place

questions.explanation: Projectors consume the event stream asynchronously (at-least-once). Users may query a read model milliseconds or seconds behind the write. Monitor lag; use write-side data for read-your-writes when UX requires it.

questions.question: How should a business correction (e.g. refund) be modeled in event sourcing?

options.text: DELETE the original PaymentAuthorized event
UPDATE the event payload in the store
Append a new compensating event such as PaymentRefunded
Overwrite the CRUD row only and skip the log

questions.explanation: Events are immutable history. Corrections are new events that describe what happened (refund, reversal). Deleting or editing past events breaks audit and replay determinism.

questions.question: Which are good reasons to adopt event sourcing? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Audit trail and temporal 'as-of' queries are requirements
You need one simple admin form with five fields
Multiple read models (search, BI, UI) from the same writes
You want to avoid thinking about schema versioning forever

questions.explanation: Event sourcing pays off when history matters and projections multiply. Simple CRUD and schema-aversion are poor fits — stored events require versioning/upcasting, and small MVPs rarely justify projector ops.

questions.question: Projectors should be designed idempotently because event delivery to consumers is often at-least-once.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Same lesson as queue consumers: retries and redelivery happen. Dedup by eventId, idempotent upserts, or inbox pattern prevents duplicate side effects when a projector processes the same event twice.
